#7543. The Hot 100 flows through social media, so Billboard is bringing YouTube data back into its charts

Billboard and YouTube have kissed and made up. A disagreement between the two companies kept the latter out of the former’s chart calculus for about a year, but Billboard is adjusting its weights to give more recognition to ad-supported streams that occur on YouTube. As a result, YouTube data will be incorporated into the Billboard charts (again) in 2027 and beyond.

Lyor Cohen, YouTube’s Global Head of Music, announced the new policy in a blog post. “We are returning to the Billboard charts starting in 2027,” Cohen wrote. “Billboard’s new methodology better reflects how fans engage with music today across both subscription and ad-supported services.”

YouTube views first became part of Billboard‘s rankings in 2013, when the music magazine recognized the growing influence of digital streams across its charts. As soon as the single-based Hot 100 and album-based 200 began factoring in YouTube-based plays, the platform’s impact became abundantly clear. At the time, Baauer’s “Harlem Shake” was the soundtrack to an inescapable viral trend, and the EDM banger shot to the top of the Hot 200 as a result.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Soon, the Hot 100 was filled with songs that were big on YouTube, and that led detractors to argue that Billboard was overemphasizing ad-supported streams. Record companies and fans could use repetitive videos to push their favorite songs to the top of the charts — and that’s exactly what they did.

In a 2017 adjustment to its chart policies, Billboard decided to weigh paid streams more heavily than ad-supported streams. As of 2025, it took 2.5 streams on an ad-supported service like YouTube to equal one stream on a subscription-based service like Spotify Premium.

Cohen protested that policy, and the squabbles eventually compelled YouTube to pull its data from the Billboard charts. “Every play should count equally,” Cohen wrote at the time.

Notably, Billboard‘s updated policy does not count all streams equally. Paid streams are still given more weight, though the gap has shrunk. Now, one paid stream will equal 1.5 ad-supported streams. That breakdown, according to Billboard, “better reflects the varied user activity occurring on these services.”

Billboard wants to do right by all its partners, but its charts couldn’t ignore YouTube forever. The platform’s impact on music consumption is undeniable, even if some of its streams only last for a few seconds. So when the Billboard charts come out on January 16, they will better reflect the pop culture landscape as it currently looks.

#7541. CTV Has Trust Issues

Around four months ago, Serge Matta, president of global ad sales at LG Ad Solutions, had a meeting with a large QSR advertiser, and he offered the CMO a guarantee.

“We said, ‘You only pay us based on incremental visits to your store as defined and measured by your independent third-party measurement provider,’” Matta shared during a session at LUMA’s Digital Media Summit earlier this week, in what felt a little like group therapy for CTV ad tech platforms.

Not so much. The QSR advertiser wasn’t convinced. “Well, how do I know I can trust them?” he asked.

“They’re your measurement partner!” Matta recalled thinking, still incredulous in his retelling.

Matta’s tale highlights a frustration that plenty of CTV sellers share. They’ve spent years positioning connected TV as a vehicle for driving outcomes, not just reach and frequency – but getting advertisers to believe it is another matter.

“We’re not there yet,” Matta said. “The promise is there, we’re pitching it, we have it, but we need advertisers to come on board.”

Ad industry vet – and self-described “recovering marketer” – Lou Paskalis piped up from the audience to venture a theory. It’s partially a perception thing.

Although there’s been an “inexorable pull down the funnel” toward performance, he said, marketers still tend to see TV as upper-funnel “hero media,” he said.

Advertisers also often don’t have the right creative for CTV, and making the creative is too expensive. “There are legacy barriers to taking full advantage,” Paskalis said, “and [CTV is] just not seen as being as performative as programmatic.”

But whatever it is that’s holding buyers back, it’s not a lack of measurement options.

Philip Inghelbrecht, CEO and co-founder of CTV ad platform Tatari, said that around 10 years ago when he started the company, people would look at him cross-eyed when he tried to talk about incrementality.

But today, there are lots of different independent third-party measurement companies that offer incrementality through a variety of models. It’s a good thing, Inghelbrecht said.

Yet, be that as it may, even the offer of a guarantee backed by independent measurement couldn’t close the deal for Matta. And sometimes the skepticism is warranted. There’s no denying that attribution is kind of a mess.

Every channel, from display to social, tries to take credit for the same conversion, said Scott Young, co-founder and chief product officer of streaming ad insertion platform Transmit.Live.

To be fair, CTV is no different in that regard, although it does bring something to the table that other channels don’t.

“You’re getting a higher rate of attention,” Young said. “Yes, you might be paying more for it, but you need exposure and attention in order to actually convert.”

But it’s also worth pointing out that this whole debate can sound rather academic to the people who control the budgets, Vinny Rinaldi, VP of client strategy and growth at The Trade Desk, reminded the room.

“Not many brands think about all the things that we talk about on a daily basis,” Rinaldi said, and he knows of what he speaks. Before joining TTD over the summer, Rinaldi spent most of his career on the brand and agency side, including multiple long stints at Hershey’s in media, marketing and strategy roles.

Marketers care about things like timing, seasonality and sales, not the ad tech plumbing underneath. And that, he argued, is why it makes sense for the DSP, not the publisher, to have the final say on when and where ads run across CTV and everywhere else.

At Hershey’s, for example, October was like its Super Bowl, but most candy sales wouldn’t happen until the last three or four days of the month in the countdown to Halloween. When he’d buy direct from publishers, however, most of the impressions would run in the first week of October, well before shoppers were thinking about Halloween candy, because the publishers were focused on monetizing their own inventory, not his business problems.

There would only be a trickle of impressions remaining by the end of the month.

If pressed, Rinaldi said, “[the publishers] would be like, ‘Well, we delivered in full, what do you mean?”

“But I wanted 95% of my spend to be the last week of October,” he said, “because it would have driven a lot more revenue for my company, not somebody else’s.”

Earning trust, it turns out, takes more than just a third-party measurement partner.

#7538. The Met Opera is using YouTube to look for a new generation of fans

Timothee Chalamet may think that no one cares about opera, but one of the most prominent opera houses in the U.S. is betting that it can find new fans for a 430-year-old art form — it just needs to look in the right place. New York’s Metropolitan Opera is delivering a YouTube live stream that will provide open access to a performance of the new work Lincoln in the Bardo.

The Lincoln in the Bardo opera, which is based on a bestselling novel by George Saunders, had its world premiere at the Met Opera last month. Now, as the 143-year-old opera company looks to expand its fan base, it is hosting a Lincoln in the Bardo live stream on its official YouTube channel. The broadcast is set to go live on November 14 and will remain available until the 18th. Beginning on November 20, the Lincoln in the Bardo stream will transition to paid formats.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

The YouTube stream isn’t just a play for new fans — it’s also a fundraiser for the host company. The Met Opera is tying its free broadcast to its Make the Met Forever fundraising campaign, which aims to bring in resources that can support Met programming through 2030. As part of the stream, viewers will be encouraged to make donations via chat.

“With the final performances of our run completely sold out, we decided to share Lincoln in the Bardo for free with our global audience,” set Meta Opera General Manager Peter Gelb in a statement provided to OperaWire. “Opera is being transformed by powerful new works like Lincoln in the Bardo, and we hope our efforts will be rewarded with donations to our Make the Met Forever fundraising campaign.”

If the Met is looking to present dramatic fare that can get younger generations excited about the medium, then Lincoln in the Bardo is an excellent choice. Saunders’ novel won the Booker Prize, and Dua Lipa‘s Service95 venture chronicled the operatic adaptation through a mini documentary. The Met Opera will stream the doc during the YouTube broadcast’s intermission.

There are several barriers that make it difficult to market opera to today’s young people, and the medium’s elitist airs present one of those roadblocks. By making Lincoln in the Bardo available to all, the Met is showing that its performances can have broad appeal — and that promoting opera doesn’t have to be as difficult as getting your son back from beyond the grave.

#7536. Liftoff Sees Big Wins Ahead For Mobile As AI Pushes Budgets Into Apps

The mobile growth marketing platform reported its second-ever quarterly earnings on Thursday after the market closed. Shares were up by almost 25% overnight after the company exceeded its revenue target and projected an optimistic profit margin outlook moving forward.

Liftoff earned $237.5 million in Q3 2026, up from $179.5 million during the same period last year. And Liftoff delivered what investors really like to see: It earned $86.7 million in profit in the quarter, after taking a $5.7 million loss in Q3 a year ago.

Liftoff is pitching itself to Wall Street as riding two tailwinds.

There’s the overall growth of the mobile economy, to which the company’s growth is pegged; that growth is being boosted by an influx of AI-generated apps.

And, secondly, there are the outsized revenue gains Liftoff earns through AI advancement compared to the relatively low investment the company must shell out for AI and data infrastructure.

LLMs are great at coding apps and are thus “lowering the barrier” for companies or individuals to churn out a serviceable app, Liftoff CEO Jeremy Bondy told investors. “In the first half of this year alone, new apps released in the Apple App Store doubled versus the prior year to roughly 560,000.”

Each of these new apps has its own demand for new users. “For Liftoff, that means more demand for user acquisition,” Bondy said.

AI products are also separately “changing where search and discovery starts” for consumers, he said.

For one thing, that means “answering more questions without sending people to a website,” Bondy said. And that new dynamic – where the open web is no longer a reliable traffic and user acquisition vehicle – incentivizes businesses to invest more into their own apps, where they still can “build direct relationships with their customers,” he added.

AI search isn’t the only thing putting pressure on the open web when it comes to user acquisition. Apple’s iOS 27 machinations are also a drag on cross-site user tracking.

AppLovin, which reported earnings a week ago, said that Apple’s obscure plan to stamp out web tracking for all iOS devices will shift marketing budgets from the mobile web to mobile apps.

And Bondy added some color, arguing that the mobile app advertising market is “drastically under-monetized” right now at about seven cents per hour, in terms of average earnings per attention time. That’s less than a sixth of what TV earns. Which means plenty of room for growth.

Speaking of growth opportunities, there is also the fact that mobile marketing gains have, to date, mostly accrued to mobile gaming apps, Bondy said.

Gaming is a category dominated by AppLovin, which is about 40x times bigger than Liftoff, in terms of the market cap. But more than half of Liftoff’s business is outside gaming, according to Bondy.

Gaming apps are a valuable source of data, though, in regard to whether someone will actually fork over money when they’re using an app (rather than just being blasted by ads without making a purchase).

“Someone who spends money in a game is also a potential high-value customer for a retailer, a social media app or a streaming service,” he said. And those are the categories in which Liftoff is positioned to grow, he said, as AppLovin has in the gaming space.

However, those nongaming apps are more prone to seasonal fluctuations than gaming apps. Which can be a good or bad thing, depending on how revenue is currently ebbing and flowing.

For instance, Liftoff rode the momentum from the FIFA World Cup and is seeing a similar surge for the NFL season, as advertisers are investing more in live sports. But it’s like surfing waves as they come, rather than riding a predictable cycle of consumer engagement ups and downs.

But Bondy noted that Liftoff has been able to convert periodic or event-based customers (like a marketer investing in promoting their app around the World Cup) into steadier, higher-spending accounts.

Liftoff had 396 customers who spent more than $100,000 in the past 12 months, Bondy said. That’s up from 362 customers at the same time last year.

Another important factor from the investor perspective is that Liftoff benefits from the AI revolution without having to financially support it.

Bondy said Liftoff has been able to greatly refine its ad targeting and personalization on the back of AI advances. The models are better at identifying a big spender from a retailer app, which makes that user a more valuable target in a gaming app, for example.

The models also now have greater longitudinal data, so they’re better at understanding long-term trends and how ROI develops over a year or more. However, the campaign returns from the week immediately after the budgets are spent are still the most important data for the model’s decision-making, Bondy said.

Meanwhile, he added, Liftoff’s profit margin expansion in the past year was propelled by the company’s relatively low cost of infrastructure and AI services. The company’s entire capital expenditures (which encompass AI and data infrastructure costs) for Q3 was $14 million, or approximately 6% of revenue.

In contrast, some companies that Liftoff competes with in mobile performance marketing (namely, Meta and Google) have committed hundreds of billions of dollars to their capex expenses.

“As a reminder, our business is capital light,” Bondy told investors yesterday – and he periodically reminded them of this fact throughout the call.

Bondy also reminded investors that Liftoff will be discontinuing its reporting of “Core Advertising” revenue going forward because advertising is now almost the entirety of the company’s business. And Liftoff has dropped the other (more expensive and subscription software-based) parts of its business, like a mobile ad network (perhaps you recall Vungle, which turned into Liftoff five years ago), and game developer analytics toolkit (an acquisition of GameRefinery).

Liftoff’s Core Advertising revenue segment earned $237 million of the company’s $237.5 in total earnings for Q3. Which illustrates why it no longer sees any need to break ads out as a separate line item.

And Bondy sees nothing but green fields ahead for AI-optimized advertising.

“Broadening the horizons in which we’re optimizing for our advertisers,” he said, “there is just a tremendous amount of space for us to continue to grow this business.”

CTV sellers are promising measurable outcomes – even guaranteed store visits – but winning advertiser trust takes more than just measurement.

#7532. With music sharing app, Samsung subsidiary Drops into the social media landscape

Short-form video feeds have transformed the recording industry, and Samsung is trying to harness contemporary consumer behaviors to get a new social media app off the ground. The new app is called Drops, and it is based around brief snippets of pop music tracks.

Drops is run by Harman, a Samsung subsidiary. The Connecticut-based company is known for distributing several consumer electronics products, including the speaker brand JBL.

With Drops, which is currently in an invite-only phase, Harman is empowering users by turning them into pop culture experts. Posts are centered around 10- to 30-second soundbites that can be paired with lyrics, album art, and other trivia related to the shared song. Users who want to check out the full tracks can follow links to services like Apple Music, and deals with rights holders (including Universal Music Group) ensure copacetic relations between Harman and the recording industry.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

The value of a musical snippet has been transformed by TikTok, which catchy choruses can become viral smashes that appear in millions of videos. TikTok is such a powerful promotional tool for artists that many now alter their top tracks so that they can fit more easily within short-form videos.

Drops, which includes tabs like “For You” and “Following,” is clearly trying to bottle some of that TikTok magic. The app’s design shows that Harman understands the depth of TikTok’s impact on the music business. ByteDance’s video app doesn’t just help songs go viral; it also cultivates musical tastemakers like Ari Elkins, who in turn help unsung artists get noticed. With a focus on sharing and curated collections called Droplists, Drops encourages users to highlight their favorite artists.

“You send a friend a song and say, ‘You have to hear this.’ Then you end up texting, ‘Skip to 1:47, that’s the best part,'” Drops General Manager Clare Hunter told TechCrunch. “The part that hits usually isn’t the first few seconds, and there wasn’t a good way to share just that moment.”

Drops arrives at a time when platforms are eager to demonstrate their influence on pop culture. YouTube, for example, has reintegrated its viewership data into the Billboard charts, while TikTok has become a key distribution and publicity partner for high-profile artists like Daddy Yankee.

By building its own community of pop music influencers, Samsung can continue its push into the creator economy. The Korean tech giant has already made moves across products like phones, smart TVs, and even ovens. Now, it has the music business in its sights — and some users in the U.S. already have the opportunity to check Drops out.

#7525. Mark Vins’ ‘Reef to Ridge’ premiered at TIFF. Now pocket.watch is on board as its distributor.

After building brands alongside some of YouTube’s biggest kid-friendly stars, pocket.watch is increasing its presence in the world of film distribution. The creator media company has come on board as the exclusive worldwide distributor and sales agent for Reef to Ridge, a nature documentary directed by Brave Wilderness Co-Founder and CEO Mark Vins.

Reef to Ridge takes viewers to the Galapagos Islands, where Vins and his crew explore unique habitats, encounter endangered species, and discuss the challenges that hinder conservation efforts around the world. The project premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF) where it was part of a showcase curated by YouTube. By highlighting projects from creators like Vins and Ziwe, YouTube showed that its biggest draws were ready for Hollywood close-ups.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

By working with Vins to give Reef to Ridge a streaming premiere, pocket.watch is solving a problem that has stunted progress for some creators with Hollywood ambitions. Major studios are eager to turn YouTube stars into feature directors, but the distributors attached to those projects have often been film industry firms like A24 and Neon. Meanwhile, creators who eschew traditional distribution can encounter some headaches, as Markiplier discovered when he attempted to bring his video game adaptation Iron Lung to YouTube.

As a creator media company, pocket.watch can pursue global distribution for a project like Reef to Ridge while also understanding the needs of a director like Vins. “Creators have built extraordinary relationships with their audiences, and there is a real opportunity to bring that connection to feature films,” said pocket.watch Founder and CEO Chris M. Williams in a statement. “Mark Vins and his team have made a visually striking, cinematic film with the ambition and scale to reach well beyond their established fanbase. We’re bringing our distribution expertise and platform partnerships to that opportunity, with more creator-led film announcements to come.”

As Williams alluded to in his statement, Reef to Ridge is just the start for pocket.watch. The media company is going to help creators realize their feature film ambitions. According to a press release, more announcements of this nature will arrive “by year’s end.”

#7523. Which social platforms do Americans use to communicate? Depends who you ask.

The Pew Research Center has delivered its annual report on U.S. social media usage, and as per usual, there are some revealing trends lurking within the demographic data. YouTube is still the most ubiquitous social platform among Americans, but beyond the top spot, the rankings differ depending on factors like age, gender, household income, and political orientation.

In last year’s Pew report, the top-ranked finishers were the platforms that best reached older Americans, and in 2026, that trend has essentially held true. YouTube, Facebook, and Instagram went 1-2-3 in the overall ranking and were the most-used social hubs in the 65-and-older age bracket.

The platforms on the rise include some apps focused on communication. Adoption of both Snapchat and WhatsApp rose 1% year-over-year, but those companies are making gains within different communities. Snapchat’s user base still skews toward female users — it reaches 30% of U.S. women and 21% of U.S. men — while WhatsApp now reaches a higher percentage of U.S. men, which wasn’t the case a year ago.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Stats related to household income are also noteworthy. Snapchat is more common in U.S. households that make less than $70,000 per year, while WhatsApp reaches its highest percentage of Americans (40%) in households that eaern at least $100,000 per year.

In general, social media use seems to be stratifying. Platforms like Facebook and TikTok tend to be more common in lower-income households. LinkedIn, as you would expect, appeals to Americans who are more well-off.

The economic polarization of U.S. social media can best be seen by examining the adoption of Nextdoor, which is a relatively new addition to Pew’s annual reports. The proportion of Americans using Nextdoor has risen by 5% over the past five years, but the community-oriented app is growing in particular communities. Only 9% of Americans in households making $30,000 or less per year use Nextdoor; in households where annual income exceeds $100,000, that percentage jumps to 23%.

Are there any clear takeaways from these economic conditions? Perhaps some marketers will want to adjust platform spend to meet target consumers where they spend the most time. But the Pew rankings also show us that U.S. social media is inherently mutable. Beyond YouTube’s hold on the top spot, there’s plenty of room for change in each year’s rankings.

And–as the name up above would imply–all the data comes from Gospel Stats. If you’re interested in learning more about Gospel–and which brands are sponsoring what creators on YouTube–click here. You can also download our YouTube 2025 Sponsorship Landscape Report here.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Boxing, golf, and football reign supreme in this week’s Gospel Stats Weekly Brand Report, with sponsorships from DAZN, DraftKings, Lowe’s, and more.

#1 The Boy Who Punched Back ?? Channel: Zack D. Films Brand: DAZN Views: 13,632,976

Zack D. Films‘ DAZN promo starts like a Dhar Mann video: A kid, relentlessly bullied, finally has enough and stands up to his schoolyard oppressors.

The Short keeps this inspirational tone, but it swings toward sports. Viewers learn the “kid” is actually world champion boxer Canelo Álvarez, and that after spending years at the top of his sport, he was defeated. Now, at 36, he wants to reclaim one of his old titles–World Boxing Council super middleweight champion–and to clinch it, he has to go up against undefeated young gun Christian Mbilli.

And, of course, that match can only be watched on DAZN. The sports-specific streamer has been in our space since the Logan Paul vs KSI days, and continues to partner with creators for special events.

#2 64 Golfers Compete For 4 Million Dollars | Internet Invitational Episode 1 Channel: Fore Play Golf, Bob Does Sports, Barstool Sports, Internet Invitational Brand: Reese’s, DraftKings, Dunkin, ZYRTEC Views: 12,095,382

And video #1 isn’t the only sports championship in the cards this week.

Fore Play Golf, Bob Does Sports, and Barstool Sports brought 64 creator golfers together for the Internet Invitational, which will pit them against each other on the green until just one puts their way to victory.

Episode 1 of this tournament is over five hours long–which is a lot of airtime for sponsors Reese’s, DraftKings, Dunkin, and ZYRTEC. We’re obviously intrigued by the tourney’s player lineup (which includes Dude Perfect‘s Tyler Toney, former Good Good-er Grant Horvat, TikToker Josh Richards, and Nelk Boys member Salim, with Barstool’s Dave Portnoy and pro golfer Kevin Kisner as rules officials), but we’re also intrigued by the brand choices. There’s some hefty companies here.

DraftKings is basically a ubiquitous presence these days no matter which sport you’re watching–or which YouTube video. It paid for more than 80 videos this week alone. Then there’s Zyrtec, which we supposes connects here because these golfers are getting snootfuls of grass out on the green. (This is the only video Zyrtec sponsored.) Dunkin and Reese’s round out the snacks-and-drinks set, and prove once again that major food n bev brands are firmly committed to spending their marketing budgets in our space.

#3 Making the worlds most extreme candy (it short-circuits my brain) Channel: NileBlue Brand: Brilliant Views: 12,475,822

He’s one of our few non-sports entrants this week, but NileBlue is still getting into the ring–and putting his tongue on the line.

His thesis is simple: candies like Warheads are trying to give the eater a truly unpleasant experience. But none of them are quite overwhelming enough.

“I think this is mostly because they’re all trying to only assault one thing at a time,” Nile says. “Which personallly, I think is a mistake, because it leaves so many completely available tastebuds completely unaffected. And what I really want is a candy that targets everything.”

That means a candy which is sour, sweet, spicy, icy, bitter, salty, and umami to the max, all at the same time.

Can he succeed? Viewers who lock in for his full 38-minute journey will be rewarded with the answer (and sponsor Brilliant will be rewarded with their watch time).

#4 LIVE with Lowes playing Madden 27, featuring Justin Jefferson! #ad Channel: MMG Brand: Lowe’s Views: 11,333,221

Our final sports video of the week is from OG Madden YouTuber MMG, who’s joined by Minnesota Vikings wide receiver Justin Jefferson for a chat and a few rounds in Madden 27.

The YouTube world and the sports world are becoming increasingly intertwined (just look at the above creator invitational, for example), so it’s not as unusual to see athletes popping up on creators’ channels, but it’s still cool every time. MMG launched his channel in 2015, and after 11 years of work, he’s sitting pretty with NFL stars.

This stream was part of the Lowe’s “Earn Your Sunday” campaign, which urges dudes to get their sh*t done around the house so they can kick back and watch the weekend games. As part of the deal, MMG gave away a signed Jefferson helmet and jersey; viewers who head over to the Lowe’s website will also see another, bigger giveaway for the “ultimate Super Bowl Sunday.” Lowe’s is definitely putting stock into making the end of this NFL season a touchdown.

BONUS #2,410 I Played Skyrim as a Lore Accurate Vampire Channel: OSK Gaming Brand: Idle Obelisk Miner Views: 124,561

In honor of everyone who waited 15 years for a name reveal, we brought in OSK Gaming and his very dedicated Skyrim playthrough as our bonus video.

Bethesda Game Studios boss Todd Howard has a contentious reputation among gamers, and OSK has another gripe for the pile: He’s pretty sure the ol’ Todd hates vampires. So what’s a guy to do if he wants to play a real vampire within the sprawling fantasy world of Skyrim? You download a boatload of mods and do it yourself. Who cares if Skyrim won’t let you be a real vampire? OSK is gonna make it happen anyway.

On his journey, he’ll actually be playing two games, thanks to his sponsor Idle Obelisk Miner. As you may expect from the name, IOM is an idle title, where you get set up and then all you have to do is check in on things every once in a while. What you might not expect is that one game title would sponsor a video about another completely unrelated game. But this is the perfect pairing. While OSK hikes across Skyrim, IOM runs in the background, so he can game while he games.

#7518. The IAB has had enough: It’s calling on platforms to standardize the definition of a “view”

When YouTube changed the way it counts public views this past August, it said its main goal was helping creators get more brand deals, and get paid more for those brand deals.

The new counts, it said, would “[give] creators a clearer picture of their overall exposure and [make] it easier to confidently express their true scale and value to brand partners and sponsors!”

But the “clearer picture” that emerged was one of inaccurate inflation. Data from Agentio showed public viewcounts over-reported actual views by 40%; experiments by individual creators like John Green, who compared his backend viewcount of one video to its public-facing count, found similar inaccuracy.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Now, the Interactive Advertising Bureau has released a report, The Creator Economy’s Next Chapter, that calls for wide standardization of what counts as a “view.”

Accurate measurement is the “fault line beneath the creator economy,” the IAB said in its report. This overall conclusion came from 53 participating industry leaders who filled out the IAB’s survey, and also from senior industry leader interviews conducted by the IAB’s Creator Economy Board.

“Measurement also sits inside problems that look like something else. Two sides who disagree on creator pricing both agree they cannot judge whether creators are paid fairly because nobody agrees what creator content is worth,” the IAB wrote. “One in eight respondents traced budget fights with leadership to measurement gaps, and a similar share said organizations withhold results because the numbers behind them are not solid enough to publish.”

We see why this is a major concern: Brands pay creators based on their reach, so when platforms like YouTube roll out changes that inflate views, marketers end up overpaying.

It might not sound bad for creators to make a little extra cash, but this situation doesn’t end well for them either. If they secure a brand deal based on inflated views, that sets a high bar for engagement that their sponsored content almost certainly will not clear. This performance gap might result in them losing their relationship with that individual brand, or with an entire agency that represents other important brands in their niche.

It’s not just marketers that told the IAB standardization is needed. “Measurement providers, who see the problem most closely, were unanimous in choosing a common definition of a view as a top priority,” the bureau said in its report.

They also have a proposed solution: “Respondents are clear about where to start. Given 11 possible standards, two-thirds (66%) chose a common definition of a view and exposure metrics across platforms,” per the report. “Each platform counts a view differently, and shared reporting format, cross-channel planning, and any comparison with video or television all depend on counting it the same way.”

Among the IAB’s respondents, another interesting data point emerged. The majority of entities that produce metrics (like platforms, marketing agencies, and measurement companies) say they are “very confident” in the accuracy of the numbers they provide.

Meanwhile brands and talent agencies both said they have zero percent confidence in numbers they receive.

The IAB says to rectify this problem, it plans to work alongside the Media Ratings Council and other “engaged industry bodies” to bring content platforms and measurement providers together so everyone can agree on cross-platform definitions of a view, an impression, reach, and watch time.

It says it hopes to secure one to two platform agreements within the first year of this effort.

If it does that, we might be looking at one of the biggest industry shifts to date, and could end up in a radically different era of social media and content creation.

35% of respondents said creators’ work split across teams and tools is not working. 33% said brands don’t understand creators’ channels. 31% cited pricing inconsistency, and 25% said agreeing on contract and deal terms is difficult.

Solutions they suggested include standard T&Cs and contracts for creator x bran deals (66% of respondents), transparency standards for agency fee disclosure (38%), and a unified creator taxonomy (31%).

#7516. New report claims TikTok Live is fastest-growing platform for game streaming

As TwitchCon descends upon San Diego, a different hub for video game streaming is celebrating its ascendance. TikTok Live is the fastest growing platform in that category, according to a new report published by the GameSquare subsidiary Hatchet.

Hatchet (previously known as Stream Hatchet) dispensed its TikTok Live status report as part of a biannual update related to the ByteDance-owned platform. During the first half of 2026, gaming streams on TikTok Live pulled in 2.5 billion hours of watch time. That traffic gave TikTok Live a 14% share of the game streaming market, pulling it even with the Stake.com-affiliated platform Kick.

Previous Hatchet reports have characterized Twitch and YouTube Gaming‘s dominant positions within the streaming landscape, but the firm’s latest dispatches have shown that TikTok Live is gaining on its market-leading rivals. While TikTok Live watch time grew 96% year-over-year, Twitch and YouTube Gaming’s respective market shares both went down.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Through properties like Hatchet, FaZe Clan, and TubeBuddy, GameSquare has made deep inroads in digital gaming communities. “Hatchet’s latest report shows just how quickly TikTok Live has established itself in gaming live-streaming,” said GameSquare CEO Justin Kenna in a statement. “Nearly doubling its gaming hours watched in a year is a clear signal that audience habits are shifting toward mobile, discovery-driven viewing.”

Kenna cited titles like Roblox, Garena Free Fire, and Mobile Legends as three major drivers of TikTok Live’s watch time uptick. Roblox led all games in terms of TikTok Live watch time during the first half of 2026; it generated 631 million hours of TikTok viewership during that period.

Roblox is a favorite of Gen Alpha gamers, while Free Fire and Mobile Legends appeal to gamers on mobile devices, especially outside of the United States. Those two data points help explain how TikTok Live has managed such a sizable gaming glow-up — it has volume none of its competitors can match. With 1.4 million creators active each day, TikTok Live’s community is nearly twice as big as Twitch’s.

That massive quantity has made TikTok Live a market leader across multiple streaming categories. Its gaming operation, however, is one of its strongest fortes, and rival platforms should be prepared to see more growth from their ByteDance-owned competitor.

#7515. The $4 million Internet Invitational might become golf’s next big thing — or another bogey

You could make the case that the most exciting golf event of 2026 involved a majority of amateurs and average joes — and the PGA wasn’t involved in the planning at all. I’m talking about the Internet Invitational, which recently wrapped up its second season by splitting a $4 million prize among the 16 members of the winning team.

The driving force behind the Internet Invitational is Dave Portnoy, the provocateur and pizza lover who is best known as the owner of Barstool Sports. To create an event that could demonstrate the influence and appeal of the “YouTube golf” scene, Portnoy teamed up with Robby Berger and his Bob Does Sports brand.

The first Internet Invitational, organized in 2025, featured Dunkin as a sponsor and a $1 million prize. The event was put on as a response to the PGA’s uneven investment in golf personalities. The Creator Classic that had signaled the PGA’s interest in digital partnerships was not held at TPC Sawgrass in 2026.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Portnoy and Berger bet that they could outdo the PGA by fully embracing golf creators, and they doubled down in 2026, when they quadrupled the size of the Internet Invitational prize. “It’s all because of Dave, man,” Barstool Sports video editor Brendan Jones told Golf magazine. “Dave puts up all this money, and that changes people. That’s not good or bad — it just changes the way that people act, right? Dave’s big thing with anything that we do at Barstool, it’s like, what are the stakes? Why do people care? How are we going to get anything out of them?”

In this case, people care because the proceedings were sillier, wackier, and more relatable than anything a PGA-sanctioned event could deliver. There were breakout stars like Paige Spiranac, wildly varied handicaps, and plenty of substance use during the tournament. And the fans loved it. Viewership hit 3.5 million during the first 24 hours and ballooned past 11 million views within a week.

“When you put the average Joe, who’s not a great golfer— that, to I think a lot of people, was riveting,” Berger told The Hollywood Reporter. “I mean, it’s kind of what Bob Does Sports was built off of.”

As exciting as the action may have been, the Internet Invitational wasn’t free from drama. Nelk member Salim Sirur‘s excessive drinking and Sam Heung Min‘s criticisms related to rules enforcement added controversy to the event’s conclusion. Given Portnoy’s controversial past and the indiscretions of some big names in the YouTube golf community (looking at you, Good Good), one wonders how long the Internet Invitational can sustain its positive momentum.

But the success of the tournament’s second iteration can’t be ignored. With the decline of LIV Golf and the presence of elite golfers on YouTube, there’s an opportunity for creators to build a viable alternative to the PGA Tour. To do that will take continued dedication from the people who made the Internet Invitational happen — and the golfers might want to cut down on the drinking, too.

#7514. Anthropic: Autonomous Systems Security Engineer

Anthropic’s mission is to create reliable, interpretable, and steerable AI systems. We want AI to be safe and beneficial for our users and for society as a whole. Our team is a quickly growing group of committed researchers, engineers, policy experts, and business leaders working together to build beneficial AI systems.

Claude is trained and served on hardware in data centers Anthropic operates and in sites partners build and run for us. DCSE secures that footprint: the sites, the hardware moving through them, and the people and vendors who touch it. You'll be the engineer who owns autonomous systems across that footprint as one security domain, from both sides: drones, ground robots and automated vehicles for patrol, inspection and moving hardware, including the security of that automation inside secure areas, and the detection systems that tell us what is flying over or operating near a site uninvited.

You set the approach, select and integrate the platforms and sensors, write the requirements vendors build to, and run what you ship, from the operating model where operators assign missions and machines carry them out to the playbook that turns a detection into an identified track and a well-evidenced handoff to whoever holds authority over the airspace. Interdiction is not part of this role. The goal is security that runs itself: coverage, fleet health and evidence verified continuously, with tools and AI agents doing the routine triage. We favor simple, standard controls and tools that can be verified over elaborate ones. We use Claude throughout our engineering workflow and expect you to as well.

You'll work with the rest of DCSE, including its physical security systems engineers and the engineers on its security monitoring platform, with Anthropic's data center operations and legal teams, and directly with site operators, equipment vendors and aviation and public safety authorities. The role is based in San Francisco, with remote applicants in the US considered, and involves regular travel to data center sites, which are critical infrastructure.

Autonomous security and inspection systems: own the drones, ground robots and other autonomous platforms for perimeter patrol, incident response and infrastructure inspection: platform selection, operating model, operator qualification, maintenance, and the data path from machine to analyst

Tools, automation and AI agents: build the integrations that carry detections, tracks, telemetry and fleet health into the team's security monitoring platform, and the tools and agents that triage detections, check fleet health and assemble evidence. When a review keeps costing people time, you build the tool or agent that retires it

Detection of uncrewed systems: engineer the sensing that tells us what is flying over or operating near a site, what it is and who needs to know: sensor selection and evaluation against live targets, per-site coverage, classification and false-alarm handling, and the playbook from first detection to handoff, with evidence retained

Security of site automation: engineer the controls on automated vehicles, robots and similar machines that move hardware or work inside secure areas: identity and access, network isolation, what they may record and where it goes, fail-secure behavior, their place in chain of custody, and acceptance before they enter a site

Health monitoring: define and test heartbeats, loss-of-coverage and lost-link alarms and fail-secure behavior, so a silent sensor or machine shows as a fault, not a quiet day

Vendor requirements and acceptance: write the requirements, evaluate against live flights and runs, and hold vendors to what they ship

Have engineered autonomous or sensing systems in the field (drones, ground robots, automated vehicles, or RF, radar or optical detection sensors): selected, integrated or secured them for an operation other people relied on, and verified what they actually do against real targets or runs rather than a datasheet

Have integrated systems you did not build (vendor APIs, SDKs, appliances, machine and sensor telemetry) into a platform that outlives any one of them

Read and review code, design the data systems behind security tooling, and build automation (often with AI coding agents) using Git and code review

Have done this work hands-on for data centers, critical infrastructure or a large hardware fleet

Own a domain end to end: set the approach, carry it through with vendors, site operators, partners and authorities, and run it as something people depend on every day

Remote pilot certification (for example FAA Part 107) and experience flying beyond visual line of sight under a waiver or exemption

Experience with counter-drone (counter-UAS) detection, airspace surveillance or air traffic data systems

Experience running a robot, drone or automated-vehicle fleet in an industrial, logistics or data center setting: fleet management, mission planning, safety cases

Experience securing embedded, operational technology or robotic systems: device identity, network segmentation, update control, logging

Experience with physical security operations at large sites, with law enforcement or aviation authorities, or at sites you did not fully control: cloud, colocation or GPU cloud operators

Have built AI agents or automation that replaced recurring manual work

The annual compensation range for this role is listed below.

For sales roles, the range provided is the role’s On Target Earnings ("OTE") range, meaning that the range includes both the sales commissions/sales bonuses target and annual base salary for the role.

Minimum education: Bachelor’s degree or an equivalent combination of education, training, and/or experience

Required field of study: A field relevant to the role as demonstrated through coursework, training, or professional experience

Minimum years of experience: Years of experience required will correlate with the internal job level requirements for the position

Location-based hybrid policy: Currently, we expect all staff to be in one of our offices at least 25% of the time. However, some roles may require more time in our offices.

Visa sponsorship: We do sponsor visas! However, we aren't able to successfully sponsor visas for every role and every candidate. But if we make you an offer, we will make every reasonable effort to get you a visa, and we retain an immigration lawyer to help with this.

We encourage you to apply even if you do not believe you meet every single qualification. Not all strong candidates will meet every single qualification as listed.  Research shows that people who identify as being from underrepresented groups are more prone to experiencing imposter syndrome and doubting the strength of their candidacy, so we urge you not to exclude yourself prematurely and to submit an application if you're interested in this work. We think AI systems like the ones we're building have enormous social and ethical implications. We think this makes representation even more important, and we strive to include a range of diverse perspectives on our team.Your safety matters to us. To protect yourself from potential scams, remember that Anthropic recruiters only contact you from @anthropic.com email addresses. In some cases, we may partner with vetted recruiting agencies who will identify themselves as working on behalf of Anthropic. Be cautious of emails from other domains. Legitimate Anthropic recruiters will never ask for money, fees, or banking information before your first day. If you're ever unsure about a communication, don't click any links—visit anthropic.com/careers directly for confirmed position openings.

We believe that the highest-impact AI research will be big science. At Anthropic we work as a single cohesive team on just a few large-scale research efforts. And we value impact — advancing our long-term goals of steerable, trustworthy AI — rather than work on smaller and more specific puzzles. We view AI research as an empirical science, which has as much in common with physics and biology as with traditional efforts in computer science. We're an extremely collaborative group, and we host frequent research discussions to ensure that we are pursuing the highest-impact work at any given time. As such, we greatly value communication skills.

The easiest way to understand our research directions is to read our recent research. This research continues many of the directions our team worked on prior to Anthropic, including: GPT-3, Circuit-Based Interpretability, Multimodal Neurons, Scaling Laws, AI & Compute, Concrete Problems in AI Safety, and Learning from Human Preferences.

Anthropic is a public benefit corporation headquartered in San Francisco. We offer competitive compensation and benefits, optional equity donation matching, generous vacation and parental leave, flexible working hours, and a lovely office space in which to collaborate with colleagues. Guidance on Candidates' AI Usage: Learn about our policy for using AI in our application process.

#7512. Have you heard? MatPat’s return, Tubi CEO’s next move, and Trisha Paytas’ payday.

Each week, we handpick a selection of stories to give you a snapshot of trends, updates, business moves, and more from around the creator industry.

This week, a beloved couple has a new channel on YouTube, a vaunted exec has a new gig, and a much-memed creator is making bank (and hitting bookshelves).

Welcome back to YouTube, Matthew and Stephanie Patrick. The man known as MatPat and his wife Stephanie haven’t shared many videos since they sold their Theorist brand nearly four years ago. But these crazy kids couldn’t stay offline forever, so they’re back with PatChat, a new channel featuring the couple’s conversations about internet culture. PatChat won’t upload nearly as frequently as the Theorist channels, and that’s ok. Let the Patricks live a little bit!

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

CNN panelist pushes back against Hasan Piker lawsuit. Piker argued that Scott Jennings defamed him by misconstruing statements that were clearly said in jest. In response, Jennings’ lawyers argued that Piker did make those statements, sarcastic or not — so they are looking to have the $72.5 million lawsuit thrown out. If commentators can be held liable for sarcasm, the internet might be in real trouble.

WhatCultureGaming launches new YouTube channel to pursue different types of content. After building a popular gaming hub, the WhatCulture team is trying something a little different with MegaWhat. The plan is to release original, personality-driven content that will give the WC team more creative freedom while still allowing them to feed the YouTube algorithm on their main channel.

Anjali Sud leaves Tubi to take point at SiriusXM. As CEO of Tubi, Sud led the transformation of the Fox-owned service, which is now a major creator hub. (She was also CEO of Vimeo before that.) Now, Sud is becoming CEO of SiriusXM, giving her a chance to work her magic in the realm of digital radio. Mike Bidgoli will take over for Sud as the new top exec at Tubi HQ.

Elevate Communications brings in TikTok vet to expand creator operations. Elevate is elevating Sam Valentine, who previously connected TikTok with luxury fashion brands as the app’s Head of Digital, Social, and Creator Services. He’ll spearhead digital and social partnerships at Elevate, where he will work with clients that are eager to build creator programs in sectors like sports, entertainment, and healthcare.

Meta brings in well-traveled exec to be the VP of its in-house content studio. After a long stint at NBC News, as well as stops at Goldman Sachs and BlackRock, Rich Latour has arrived at Meta. He will be put in charge of a studio that emphasizes Meta’s brand and highlights its impact across various communities and industries.

Trisha Paytas has a book out (and she makes $100,000 a week on YouTube). While promoting her memoir Crying on the Kitchen Floor, which was recently published by Hachette, Paytas told Andy Cohen that her YouTube earnings can hit six figures during a good week. Oh, and she also has a new dating show that is rolling out on Tubi. Slow down, Trish!

Hulu taps Tinx to revive The Circle (now with TikTok voting). The creator born Christina Najjar is taking the hosting role in a new version of the reality competition series that previously aired on Netflix. Tinx will have big shoes to fill replacing previous host Michelle Buteau, but with help from the voting audience, she can ensure that the Circle revival doesn’t miss a beat.

The first Clio Creator Awards will fete Dhar Mann. Actor Terry Crews will host as the notable advertising award ceremony expands to the realm of creator content. Dhar Mann, YouTube moralist and engineer of many a brand partnership, will receive an inaugural honorary award at the new ceremony.

Kind works with a Savannah Banana to sell a TikTok-exclusive foodstuff. Baseball player Jackson Olson has amassed a significant TikTok following after getting a roster spot on the best-known “Banana Ball” team. Olson is now parlaying his influence to sell a new type of Kind bar that celebrates World Kindness Day — and is only available for purchase via TikTok Shop.

GTA VI codes are flying around on Kick and Twitch ahead of launch day. All of the major platforms want creators to play GTA VI on their services once the game launches, and giving out free copies is a good way to engender that loyalty. At this point, I’m wondering if GTA VI will be able to live up to its immersurable hype, or if viewers will tire of it after it because the main topic of conversation everywhere.

Barbie and Hot Wheels are on TikTok Shop this holiday season. TikTok continues to onboard name brands as it prepares for its most lucrative holiday season shopping spree. So if someone on your list has their eyes on some Mattel products, deals on those items will be hitting TikTok Shop in no time.

Celebs are consenting to having their voices cloned for AI ads. Ogilvy and CAA have teamed up for a partnership that will make a-list talent more accessible for advertisers and agencies that rely on generative AI pipelines. George Clooney is a CAA client, but if he goes along with this, I’m going to have no choice but to start calling him George Cloney.

Shaq is good at dunking, but can he hide in plain sight? The Big Diesel has a new gig: An ABC series that will ask contestants to hide the 7’1″ goliath in plain sight. I think, to be fair, the contestants should get to start by hiding Kevin Hart before working their way up to Shaq.

Another impulse spending deterrent is taking off in China. The WeChat mini-app dubbed ‘Wallet, Please Wait’ lets users decide whether strangers will be able to hold off on big purchases. I would be more interested in app that lets me vote on whether a stranger should be able to tell a stranger how to spend their money.

#7510. In the AI age, publishers who understand what readers want will do best, a new report argues

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

AI inverts the traditional journalism hierarchy: Instead of reporters gathering information, editors deciding how to present it, and newsrooms releasing the same final story to everyone, AI agents deliver what readers ask for, refining or expanding on information as requested.

It’s “an interactive process in a way the current news system isn’t,” write the authors of “The Three-Layer Cake: Public-Interest Information in an AI-Intermediated Age,” released Wednesday by the Tow-Knight Center for Journalism Futures at the Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at CUNY. (The cake’s three layers are “the products that identify what people want to know, the systems that synthesize answers, and the organizations that produce the underlying reporting.”)

Some interesting ideas from the report by Gina Chua and Adiel Kaplan:

This new age may be better for some readers. The authors write:

There are people the old system never reached, or never reached well. A parent who hears of school budget cuts may want to know if their child’s elementary school art class will survive. No newsroom would assign that story. It matters to a handful of families whose children attend a single school, and the exact answer is uncertain. A well-designed AI system could pull together what is known from reporting and context and offer a nuanced response — fulfilling an information need that previously did not have enough economic power to be met directly.

Similarly, minority communities whose concerns didn’t rise to the level of interest of a city newspaper might have rarely seen their perspectives reflected in coverage in the past. Coverage in the mainstream media of the AIDS epidemic in the early 1980s was often focused on the risk to the heterosexual population rather than on the gay community it ravaged. An AI system that can access information from and about underserved communities could rectify that.

Publishers opting out could make the information environment worse. If news organizations seek to prevent AI from using their content, they may contribute to a poorer “information commons,” the authors argue. It “works as a strategy for individual organizations, but cedes the broader mission of providing information to the vast majority of the public to others who may not have the public’s interests at heart.”

Scoops and exclusives are a “luxury” — and they’re losing value fast.

Even a pivot to investigative reporting, as important a public good as that is, is not necessarily a solution. Much of investigative journalism is summarizable once it is published, even if the original story breaks important news and is a delight to read. As Francesco Marconi noted, a multi-month investigation could cost a newsroom $200,000 in resources, then drop in economic value to close to zero within minutes of publication. Both investigations and scoops can have huge social value and help build a brand, but economically, they provide little lasting value to their newsrooms — and even less so in an AI-intermediated landscape. “Commoditized news” isn’t saving anyone. Publishers have to make “hard choices” about what they’ll cover, the authors write: In an AI-intermediated world, commoditized news carries little value, especially if it’s already available in some other form. That’s not to say that day-to-day coverage of municipal government, a core task of many local newsrooms, should go away; only that its coverage needs to be differentiated from what could be found elsewhere or summarized from a meeting transcript, for it to hold value. Differentiation might involve adding context to the coverage through original reporting, or asking questions that wouldn’t otherwise be asked at a press conference. The deeper and more specialized a newsroom’s area of coverage and expertise is, the less likely it is to be duplicated by other organizations — and that provides both pricing power and closer links to the communities that value such information.

“Commoditized news” isn’t saving anyone. Publishers have to make “hard choices” about what they’ll cover, the authors write:

In an AI-intermediated world, commoditized news carries little value, especially if it’s already available in some other form. That’s not to say that day-to-day coverage of municipal government, a core task of many local newsrooms, should go away; only that its coverage needs to be differentiated from what could be found elsewhere or summarized from a meeting transcript, for it to hold value. Differentiation might involve adding context to the coverage through original reporting, or asking questions that wouldn’t otherwise be asked at a press conference.

The deeper and more specialized a newsroom’s area of coverage and expertise is, the less likely it is to be duplicated by other organizations — and that provides both pricing power and closer links to the communities that value such information.

The report is here. Read excerpts from a talk that coauthor Chua gave to Nieman Fellows here.

#7508. The Ringer bets on Substack’s network over its own website

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Once synonymous with independent writers, Substack is increasingly home to established publishers.

“Very interesting that The Ringer’s writers write on Substack and not…The Ringer.” “What’s the point of the website then?” “Hold up. You’re telling me The Ringer would rather make money on writing than not make money on writing?”

These were some of the responses after The Ringer’s Zach Lowe announced his new newsletter. The Lowe Post, which covers the NBA, joins The Ringer’s Sean Fennessey, Tom Pelissero, and Bryan Curtis on Substack. (The Lowe Post is $10 a month, and has already become one of Substack’s bestselling sports newsletters. Fennessey’s newsletter is $5 a month; Pelissero’s is $8 a month, and Curtis’s is free.)

Though podcasting has been his main gig for a while now, Zach Lowe is one of the best sports writers in the country — witty, warm-hearted, and a true lover of basketball and the Mets. In his inaugural newsletter, he wrote about how he feels his sports analysis loses a step when he’s only talking, not writing.

On the one hand, of course Lowe should have a newsletter. But his Substack, and those of his colleagues, are not independent side hustles. Each has Spotify and The Ringer branding.

As a digital media business, The Ringer has always been flexible and opportunistic. It was initially published on Medium when it launched in 2016. The publication moved to an ad and tech partnership with Vox in 2017. It was acquired by Spotify for $250 million in 2020 and, five years later, signed a distribution deal with Netflix to bring some of its video podcasts (including The Bill Simmons Show, The Zach Lowe Show, and The Rewatchables) to the platform. The website has always been free to read.

The Ringer declined to comment on its Substack strategy and would not tell me whether the writers receive a share of subscription revenue. (The lack of comment has garnered its own press coverage.) Though The Ringer has referred to the new newsletters as being in “partnership” with Substack, there’s no separate financial relationship between the two companies, Substack confirmed.

If you find this a little strange, you’re not wrong. The Substack-Ringer whatever-this-is is a confusing move that is raising a lot of very 2026 questions. Here are some things I’m wondering.

While Grantland — the beloved sports writing site created by Ringer founder Bill Simmons in 2011 and shuttered by ESPN in 2015 — was known for its long-form journalism, The Ringer is all-in on podcasts. Simmons jokes on nearly every episode of his own show that his “fingers stopped working” years ago and that his days writing columns are behind him.

Today, most of the links on The Ringer’s homepage will bring you somewhere else. The homepage’s function is closer to a landing page or linktree than a news website. Many links redirect to Spotify, where listeners can watch or listen to Ringer podcasts. Now, with the newsletter launches, several links whisk you off The Ringer and over to Substack.

Burned by Facebook and forever-shifting algorithmic winds, many publishers have focused on building on their own channels in recent years. The theory is that direct-to-reader news products like newsletters, apps, and events will help publishers control audience connections and insulate them from inevitable platform pivots.

But though Substack was once synonymous with independent writers, its perks are luring more and more established publications onto the platform. Some, like The Ringer, are sharing Substack-exclusive content. Others, like New York magazine and The Wall Street Journal, are redistributing work that exists elsewhere on the internet.

One major pull? Substack has morphed into a full-on social media platform, albeit one where publishers can directly monetize and capture email addresses for themselves.

In the past six months, the app has generated nearly 800,000 paid subscriptions, according to Substack, and more than half of those subscriptions came directly from its Twitter-like Notes feed. Network effects account for more than half of all subscriptions on the platform and about 30% of paid subscriptions, a spokesperson said.

Media journalist Simon Owens has been tracking the rise of traditional media outlets on Substack (on Substack, naturally).

“Open web” is an ill-defined concept. Sometimes people use it to mean the public portion of the internet that’s indexable by search engines. Others mean, basically, websites — anything you can reach on a web browser at a URL. Whatever the semantics, people have been shoveling dirt on “the open web” for years. (This New York Times obituary noting the rise of paywalls, apps, and tiers of access was published back in 2010.) But the death notices have picked up with the rise of AI.

RELATED ARTICLESearch traffic has declined so much that some publishers are considering opting out of Google entirelyNeel DhaneshaJuly 22, 2026Google Search referrals to publisher websites are down 40.2% year over year, according to Chartbeat. And AI chatbots are not sending users to news sites. Referrals from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, and the like were just 0.01% of traffic to publishers and declining, Chartbeat found.

Even before it was acquired by Spotify, The Ringer’s primary business was podcasts, so it’s never been as reliant on search as text-first publishers. The Ringer can afford to deprioritize its website more than most. But all kinds of publishers are having to respond to a real shift in the way people consume news and content.

RELATED ARTICLEWhat’s it take to make a great daily newsletter? Axios’ Kendall Baker is planning to bring one to Yahoo SportsJoshua BentonAugust 17, 2023Kendall Baker, senior writer and head of newsletters for Yahoo Sports, knows a thing or two about email newsletters. He says The Ringer’s move exemplifies a news consumption trend that’s only picking up speed.

“Most people’s general way of finding information or consuming information online is that they’re opening their phone and going straight to a social media app and starting to scroll,” Baker said.

Another app that most U.S. adults open up every day? Their email.

“If I want an engaged audience on a daily basis, relying on them coming to find me versus going to them would be silly — and it’s becoming more and more silly,” he said. “I think that’s partially what’s driving this. Newsletters are an obvious solution there.”

The Ringer’s move is also a bet on the strength of individual personalities. Substack doesn’t (yet) offer bundles, so a reader who wants all of The Ringer’s paid Substack content will have to fork over something like $23/month — more than a subscription to New York magazine or Apple News and a little less than a full New York Times bundle. Even with the strong parasocial relationships The Ringer enjoys — enough to fuel many, many subreddits — the pricing was a common complaint online.

Many publishers will not want to cannibalize pricier subscriptions by selling access to a single popular writer. Offering a whole-site subscription also lets readers discover (and hopefully fall in love with!) more of your content.

“It seems in the Substack era, you’re writing for people who really like you,” Simmons said on a recent podcast about sportswriting. “And you’re getting that audience but then, how do you pull other people in? That’s going to be the big question over the next five to 10 years.”

“Obviously we have a lot of writing on The Ringer dot com that we’re very proud of,” Simmons added, pointing to a NFL Take-O-Meter piece by The Ringer’s Austin Gayle. “But will it ever be like 2011 again? I don’t know.”

“You mean, when we launched Grantland?” The Ringer’s Bryan Curtis asked.

“No, just that era. How many writers were coming up — the energy behind it, and all the different styles,” Simmons said. “I wonder if we’ll ever have that many writers again trying that many different things.”

The largest news publishing trade association in the United States is calling on Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg to suspend the implementation of the company’s new commercial terms of service, set to go into effect on October 30.

In an open letter to Zuckerberg published Thursday, News/Media Alliance’s president and CEO Danielle Coffey wrote that Meta should “withdraw these terms and should hold discussions around future changes with NMA and publishers.”

The terms, first reported by Nieman Lab on October 15, would allow for the mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. There is currently no option to opt out. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” But legal experts told Nieman Lab the revised terms would still permit mass scraping.

“News publishers will be forced into providing their valuable journalism to support the development of products that may be used to compete with them for readers and advertisers, under duress and without compensation,” Coffey said in her letter. “It is wholly unreasonable for the mere use of a Meta business account to require publishers to grant unrestricted access to their websites (and even content posted by their users), for the benefit of Meta to develop its business products.”

NMA represents more than 2,000 news publishers in the United States. The discussions, Coffey said, should focus on four core issues:

(i) the specific Meta Company Products and uses for which Meta would like to use publishers’ scraped content;

(ii) how publishers can opt in to permit scraping, separate from obtaining access to Meta’s business products;

(iii) the specific crawlers, fetchers, or other bots that will be utilized;

(iv) how Meta will ensure publishers’ robots.txt files, registration walls, or paywalls are respected.

Coffey requested a public response from Zuckerberg to the letter by October 26, and noted that if “in the event Meta adopts these revised terms over our members’ express objections, our members do not consent to them and reserve all of their legal rights.”

The World Association of News Publishers (WAN-IFRA) sent a similar letter to Meta’s chief global affairs officer Joel Kaplan on Thursday, while adding its concern about Meta’s implementation of its new subscription service, Meta One, which requires users to pay a fee to post links on Meta platforms. WAN-IFRA’s membership spans 20,000 publishers in 120 countries around the world.

The Center for Media and Digital Governance (CMDG) at the Open Markets Institute published its own statement on Thursday, saying that regulators in the United States should take immediate action to “stop Meta from exploiting publishers around the world.”

“If Meta gets away with this, every dominant technology company will have a blueprint for doing the same,” said CMDG director Courtney Radsch. “Regulators have an opportunity to draw a line now, before the next generation of AI monopolies is built on the uncompensated work of journalists, publishers, and creators.”

On Thursday morning, the Movement for an Open Web (MOW) — a U.K. nonprofit organization that advocates for an accessible internet — filed formal complaints with the U.K. Competition and Markets Authority and the European Commission’s Directorate General for Competition, calling the terms “unfair,” and “exploitative” and saying they “threaten to cause immediate and irreparable harm to businesses.”

“The terms go live in a few days’ time, and once they’re in force the damage will be done — you can’t unscrape that content,” said Tim Cowen, a MOW cofounder.

MOW’s complaints follow comments from CMA executive director for digital markets Will Hayter, who said during a parliamentary committee session on Tuesday that he had sent a letter to Meta and scheduled a meeting with company representatives to learn more about the terms. In Germany, the German Association of Free Press and the Federal Association of Digital Publishers also sent a joint letter to the European Commission, calling on the institution to block the new terms from going into effect until it conducted a complete review.

On Wednesday, four European press associations — the European Magazine Media Association, the European Newspaper Publishers’ Association, the European Press Council, and News Media Europe — sent a joint letter to the European Commission and its heads of technology and competition. The letter, viewed by Nieman Lab, claims that Meta’s new terms violate the European Union’s Digital Markets Act, a law passed in 2020 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region.

The joint letter calls on the Commission to block the terms from “taking effect in their current wording — or in any wording producing identical or similar effects — to safeguard publishers’ rights.”

“Publishers, whose content has long been subject to sweeping unfair and unlawful exploitation by dominant gatekeepers, including for AI-related purposes, thus face an unacceptable choice: abandon a key distribution channel or consent to the exploitation of their professional content without negotiation, licensing and remuneration,” the letter reads. “These conditions could also undermine publishers’ rights in ongoing or future AI-related legal proceedings.”

RELATED ARTICLEMeta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts sayAndrew DeckOctober 15, 2026The Association of Information Media (AMI) in Spain, which represents more than 100 news outlets in the country, echoed its support of the letter in a statement on Thursday.

“Technological innovation and the development of artificial intelligence cannot come at the expense of content creators’ rights or the economic viability of professional journalism,” the AMI statement reads in part. “Defending publishers’ rights does not mean hindering innovation, but rather ensuring that it develops while respecting the law, competition, and media pluralism.”
